title: SteadyFlow: GPU Occupancy Probing and Priority Flow Sketch
body:
Purpose and high-level idea:

This note sketches an alternative admission/routing approach called SteadyFlow that aims to: smooth transient bursts, preserve tail latency SLOs, and maintain high sustained GPU utilization across multi-region fleets. The approach combines short-duration occupancy probes, soft priority windows, credit-pool shaping (credit pools are analogous to token buckets but managed hierarchically), and cooperative control-plane feedback to avoid thrash and unnecessary cross-region spillovers.

Motivation / why this differs from other sketches:
- Many prior notes focus on strict token-bucket admission or queue-slope shaping. SteadyFlow emphasizes frequent light-weight occupancy probes plus short-lived priority windows to make better decisions when utilization and queue depth signals disagree.
- Probe-driven decisions reduce the need for heavy conservative shedding while enabling ephemeral overload detection (e.g., sudden 10s spikes) without long cooldowns.
- Credit pools let us express both per-tenant guarantees and opportunistic spare capacity usage with fast reclaim semantics.

Key concepts (glossary):
- credit pool: numeric credits assigned to a tenant/route for a timeslice. Credits replenish periodically. Unlike classic token buckets, credits can be borrowed across short windows with fast revocation by the local admission controller.
- occupancy probe: a micro-request (probe) sent internally to a serving node or GPU instance to measure effective throughput/latency under current conditions. Probes are very small and instrumentation-only (no billing).
- priority window: a short time window (50–500ms) during which a route is allowed higher concurrency based on successful probe outcomes and available credits.
- probe score: combined heuristic (0..1) from recent probe RTTs, GPU SM utilization percentile, and queue depth trend.

Signals used:
- GPU-level: sm_util (short-term percentile), dram_bw, temperature; also kernel queue occupancy if available from runtime.
- Serving-level: incoming queue length, average queue wait-time, active KV cache hits, tail tokenization cost distribution.
- Control-plane: regional residual capacity score (based on measured throughput and headroom), recent cross-region egress cost and latency penalty.

Probe mechanics:
- Frequency: route-level probes at configurable base frequency (e.g., 1 probe / 1000 requests or 1 probe every 200ms for hot routes) with exponential backoff for cold routes.
- Probe execution path: probes are routed to candidate serving nodes (local preferred). They are scheduled with highest priority to avoid being queued behind heavy work; timeouts are short (50–100ms).
- Probe interpretation: a successful low-latency probe increases the probe score and may open a priority window; failed or slow probes decrement the probe score and reduce concurrency budgets. Use EWMA on probe RTTs (alpha=0.2) and combine with 95th percentile sm_util over 30s windows to compute probe score.

Credit pool semantics:
- Each tenant/route gets a soft guaranteed baseline credit (G) and a burst credit (B) that leaks faster. Credits replenish on 1s tick (or adaptive tick depending on workload).
- Borrowing & revocation: if a tenant is using borrowed credits (beyond G), the local admission controller can revoke borrowed credits within a 100–300ms window when probes indicate degradation, forcing early-drop or downgrade to a cheaper model variant.
- Hierarchy: credits exist at the node, AZ, and regional tiers. Credits flow upward (unused node credits counted toward AZ spare) but borrow revocation decisions are local-first to limit blast radius.

Priority windows and flow control:
- When probe score crosses a threshold (0.6 by default) and sufficient credits exist, open a priority window for the route for T_win ms (default 200ms). During the window: allow a higher concurrency ceiling (soft limit) and prefer placement on nodes with low sm_util percentiles.
- Windows are overlapping and short to reduce on/off oscillation. The system limits the number of concurrent priority windows per node to avoid piling up boosted requests.

Backpressure & graceful degradation:
- Three de-escalation modes, in order of preference: 1) queue delay hints to client (X-Estimate-Wait), 2) downgrade to lighter model variant / quantized flavor automatically, 3) probabilistic early drop with bias toward non-critical tenants.
- Early drop uses a fast Bernoulli drop whose probability increases with sm_util > high_threshold and queue_depth > q_threshold. Drop decisions respect tenant SLAs: guaranteed-tone tenants get lower drop probability.

Multi-region coordination and control-plane interactions:
- Local controllers make immediate decisions using local probes and credits; the regional control-plane receives periodic summaries (30s–1m) of residual capacity and probe-failure rates.
- On cross-region spillover: prefer region with matching model variant and acceptable egress latency budget. Spill decisions are gated by a regional spill score combining residual capacity and egress penalty.
- To avoid control-plane oscillation, add dampening: only change region-level routing when trend persists for >= 90s or when residual capacity delta exceeds a configured hysteresis.

Operational notes & observability:
- Telemetry to emit for each request: probe_taken (bool), probe_score_at_request, credit_state (G/B/borrowed), priority_window_id, chosen_node_id, sm_util_at_node, queue_wait_ms.
- Dashboards: rolling distribution of probe scores, borrowed-credit fraction, priority window count, evicted-because-of-revocation events, and cross-region spill rate.
- SLO/alerts: alert if borrowed-credit fraction exceeds 30% sustained for 2min, or if probe success rate falls below 80% for critical routes.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Probe floods adding load: probes are very small and capped per-node; if probes become noisy, reduce frequency and aggregate using sample windows.
- Misleading probes (fast local but global slow): ensure probe path mirrors actual work path including KV cache lookups; add synthetic probe variants that exercise heavier code-path occasionally.
- Rapid oscillation in priority windows: mitigate with randomized jitter on window start times and a cumulative cooldown per-route.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact credit replenishment math: linear vs. leaky bucket vs. adaptive rate based on recent consumption — short experiment needed.
- Optimal probe sizing: how substantive must a probe be to reflect true tail behavior? small RNG of probe types needed.
- Integration with existing token-bucket playbooks: gradual migration or parallel operation? Suggest a canary where a small set of routes use SteadyFlow while token-bucket remains default.
- CPU vs GPU signal fusion: how to weight SM utilization vs. kernel queue occupancy vs. host-side queue? Need tracer experiments.

Short rollout plan (canary -> staged):
1) Instrument probe and emit probe_score metric roofed behind feature flag (2 weeks).
2) Implement local credit pool + priority window logic in a sidecar/agent; run in read-only mode to collect simulated decisions (1 month).
3) Canary on low-risk customer routes with only priority-window enabling and no revocation (2–4 weeks).
4) Enable fast revocation and downgrade in controlled set (another 2–4 weeks).

Checklist before broader rollout:
- [ ] Simulation harness for mixed workloads (chat, embed, rerank) to validate borrowed-credit risk.
- [ ] E2E tracing for probe->decision->outcome to compute true probe predictive power.
- [ ] SRE runbook for early drop vs downgrade incidents.
- [ ] Cost analysis: does SteadyFlow reduce cross-region egress vs naive spill?

Notes / references:
- Related internal tickets: JIRA PLAT-8123 (linked above) contains experiment logs from a small internal trial in May 2025.
- Compare and contrast: Where token-bucket policies are simpler to reason about for billing, SteadyFlow trades some simplicity for responsiveness and lower unnecessary long-term shedding.

If helpful, I can draft a minimal proto for the credit-pool state and probe_score schema to slot into the agent; next step would be a tiny RFC and a simulated cluster test.
